chapter.name: Algebra Play
chapter.blurb: Using algebra to explain and invent 'think of a number' and date-guessing tricks, number pyramids, calendar and shape grids, the largest-product digit puzzle, and divisibility tricks based on digit reversal, cyclic rotation and repetition.

scope_in.item: Representing a 'think of a number' trick as an algebraic expression in one variable x, and simplifying it to show whether the result is a fixed constant or still depends on x
Modifying the steps of a 'think of a number' trick (e.g. changing the constant added) so that it produces a different fixed final answer

The date-guessing trick: writing algebraic expressions in two letters, month M and day D (5M, 5M+6, 20M+24, 20M+33, 100M+165, 100M+165+D), and decoding a reported total back into the original month and day
The number pyramid rule (each entry is the sum of the two entries directly below it); filling numeric pyramids of 2, 3 and 4 rows given the bottom row
Writing and using algebraic expressions for the topmost entry of a pyramid in terms of letter-numbers in the bottom row (a+b for 2 rows, a+2b+c for 3 rows, a+3b+3c+d for 4 rows)
The first few Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers used as the bottom row of a pyramid, and reasoning about the resulting entries
Setting up and solving linear equations for an unknown letter-number in a pyramid from the top total and one other clue (e.g. a+b=60, 12+c=a, c+8=b)
Calendar Magic: expressing the four entries of a 2x2 calendar grid in terms of the top-left value a (a, a+1, a+7, a+8), forming and solving 4a+16 equals a given sum

Algebra Grids: shapes representing unknown numbers, each row's shapes summing to a given total, and solving the resulting equations for each shape's value (grids of two or three distinct shapes, two or three rows)

Arranging three given digits into a (2-digit) x (1-digit) multiplication to find the largest possible product, first by comparing all six arrangements and then by the algebraic proof that the largest digit should be the multiplier and the remaining two digits placed in decreasing order
Writing a 2-digit number as 10a+b and its digit-reversal as 10b+a, and proving algebraically that their difference is always a multiple of 9 and their sum is always a multiple of 11
Writing a 3-digit number as 100a+10b+c, forming its two cyclic digit-rotations, and proving algebraically that the sum of all three is always a multiple of 37 (and of 3)
Recognising that repeating a 3-digit number to form a 6-digit number is equivalent to multiplying by 1001 = 7 x 11 x 13, so dividing successively by 7, 11 and 13 recovers the original number

scope_out.item: Designing an entirely new two-variable trick with different coefficients from scratch (the book's 'invent your own trick' prompts)
scope_out.reason: Open-ended creative design of new coefficient sequences has no fixed answer to check against; only the book's own date-trick structure and its numeric decoding are treated as testable content

scope_out.item: General nth-row or nth-term proofs for arbitrary pyramid height, beyond the 2, 3 and 4-row cases the book works through
scope_out.reason: The book poses these as open pattern-exploration questions (Figure It Out items 4-6 on page 140) without a worked proof; testing them as fixed-answer items would go beyond what the book itself demonstrates

scope_out.item: Calendar grids other than a plain 2x2 block (the book's 'create your own grid of a different size and shape' prompt), and irregular or non-rectangular grid shapes
scope_out.reason: These are open creative prompts with no single fixed grid to check answers against

scope_out.item: Algebra Grids with more than three distinct unknown shapes or more than three rows
scope_out.reason: The book's own worked examples and practice grids stay at two or three shapes across two or three rows; larger systems are not shown or practised in this chapter

scope_out.item: Smallest-product versions of the digit-arrangement puzzle
scope_out.reason: The chapter's heading and every worked example is about the LARGEST product only; a smallest-product question, while solvable with the same technique, is not something this chapter poses

scope_out.item: The genie-and-coins riddle, the horses-and-hens problem, the mother-and-daughter age problem, the dosa-cart pricing problem, the cowherds'-cows problem, and the odd-number-fraction-sequence pattern (Figure It Out items 5 to 10 on pages 145-146)
scope_out.reason: These are independent linear-equation word problems bundled at the end of the chapter under general practice; they exercise equation-solving skills taught elsewhere in the book, not the digit-representation divisibility-trick reasoning that section 6.6 is actually about, and folding them into that concept would blur its boundary
It mirrors Part I's hegp1ps.pdf appendix and is out of scope for the same reason: it is a separate cumulative problem bank, not part of this chapter's own content

concepts.name: Think of a Number tricks with one variable
concepts.description: Representing a 'think of a number' trick as an algebraic expression in one variable and simplifying it to show whether the result depends on the starting number.
concepts.idea: If we call the unknown starting number x, each instruction in the trick becomes an algebraic operation on x; simplifying the resulting expression often makes the x cancel out, leaving a fixed number.
concepts.rule: To explain a 'think of a number' trick, write the starting number as x, translate every step into an expression in x, and simplify. If x cancels out, the final result is the same for every starting number; if x remains, the result still depends on the number chosen.
concepts.example: Think of a number x. Double it: 2x. Add four: 2x + 4. Divide by two: x + 2. Subtract the original number: x + 2 - x = 2. The result is always 2, whatever x is.

questions.q: In the trick 'think of a number, double it, add four, divide by two, subtract the number you first thought of', the starting number is written algebraically as
questions.a: x

questions.q: 'Double it' applied to the letter-number x is written as
questions.a: 2x

questions.q: In the trick, after doubling x and adding four, the expression becomes ____.
After 'divide by two' is applied to the expression 2x + 4, the result simplifies to
Why does the final result of the classic trick (double, add four, halve, subtract the original number) always come out the same, no matter what number you start with?
questions.a: Because the letter x cancels out when the expression is simplified
o: Because the letter x cancels out when the expression is simplified
Because doubling and halving always give zero
Because four is an even number

questions.q: In the expression x + 2 - x, what happens to the letter-number x?
questions.a: It cancels out, leaving just 2

questions.q: Explain why subtracting the original number you thought of is the key step that makes a 'think of a number' trick always give the same answer.
questions.a: Because it removes the letter x from the simplified expression, leaving only the fixed numbers that were added or divided along the way.
s: States that this step removes or cancels the x term
Explains that only the fixed numbers remain, giving a constant result

questions.q: A trick is: think of a number x, add six, multiply by two, subtract twelve, divide by two. Which of these is NOT one of the correct intermediate expressions produced while simplifying this trick?
A trick is: think of a number, add six, multiply by two, subtract twelve, divide by two. Simplify the expression using x for the starting number, and state the final result.
questions.a: x + 6, then 2x + 12, then 2x, then x. The final result equals the number you started with, not a fixed constant.
s: Correctly simplifies through each step to reach 2x before the final division
States that the final result equals x, the original number

questions.q: Aliya invents a trick: think of a number, add ten, then subtract the original number. Which expression is left after simplifying?
Think of a number x, triple it, then subtract the original number twice (that is, subtract x, then subtract x again). The simplified expression is ____.
questions.a: x

questions.q: A trick is: think of a number, add eight, multiply by three, subtract twenty-four. What does the simplified expression equal?
questions.a: 3x

questions.q: Modify the classic trick (think of a number, double it, add four, divide by two, subtract the original number) so that the final answer is always 5 instead of 2. State the one change you would make.
questions.a: Change 'add four' to 'add ten': doubling x gives 2x, adding ten gives 2x + 10, dividing by two gives x + 5, and subtracting the original number x leaves 5.
s: Identifies that changing the added constant is the key modification
Gives a correct new constant (e.g. add ten) and verifies the result is 5

questions.q: A trick says: think of a number, multiply by four, add the original number three times (that is, add x, add x, add x), then divide by seven. Simplify and state the result.
questions.a: 4x, then 4x + x + x + x = 7x, then divided by 7 gives x. The result equals the original number.
s: Correctly adds x three times to 4x to reach 7x
Divides by 7 to correctly get x, the original number

questions.q: Design your own 'think of a number' trick using exactly four steps (a multiplication, an addition, a division, and a subtraction of the original number) so that the final answer is always 7. Write the steps, the algebraic simplification, and check it with the starting number 6.
questions.a: Example: think of a number x, multiply by 2 (2x), add 14 (2x + 14), divide by 2 (x + 7), subtract the original number (7). Check with x = 6: 6 doubles to 12, plus 14 is 26, divided by 2 is 13, minus 6 is 7.
s: Writes four valid steps (multiply, add, divide, subtract original) with correct constants
Simplifies the expression algebraically in x to show it equals 7
Checks correctly with the starting number 6

questions.q: Assertion (A): The trick 'think of a number, double it, add four, divide by two, subtract the original number' always gives 2. Reason (R): when simplified algebraically, the letter x cancels out, leaving only 2.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Consider: (I) In the expression x + 2 - x, the terms with x cancel because they have opposite signs. (II) Any 'think of a number' trick that ends by subtracting the original number will always give a fixed constant answer. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A trick is: think of a number, multiply it by itself (square it), subtract four times the number, then add four. A friend claims this trick's algebraic form simplifies to (x - 2) squared, and says the final answer is always the same. Is the friend right? Explain using algebra, and test with two different starting numbers.
questions.a: The expression is x squared - 4x + 4, which does equal (x - 2) squared. But this is NOT a constant, since its value still changes with x (for example x = 6 gives 16, x = 10 gives 64). So the friend is only half right: the algebraic identity is correct, but the trick does not give a fixed answer, unlike the linear tricks in this chapter.
s: Confirms x squared - 4x + 4 equals (x - 2) squared algebraically
Recognises this expression is not a constant since it still contains x
Tests with two different starting numbers and shows the results differ

questions.q: A student simplifies the trick 'think of a number, double it, add four, divide by two, subtract the original number' as follows: 2x, then 2x+4, then x+4, then x+4-x=4. Identify the student's mistake and give the correct final answer.
questions.a: The student divided only the 2x term by two and forgot to divide the +4 as well, writing x+4 instead of x+2. The correct final answer is 2.
s: Identifies that the student failed to divide the +4 by two as well
States the correct final answer, 2

questions.q: Invent your own 'think of a number' trick with at least four steps that always ends in the number 9. Write out the steps in words, show the algebraic simplification, and verify it works for the starting number 15.
questions.a: Example: think of a number x; multiply by three (3x); add nine (3x + 9); subtract three times the original number (3x + 9 - 3x = 9). Check with x = 15: 15 x 3 = 45, plus 9 is 54, minus 3 x 15 = 45, gives 9.
s: Writes at least four clear steps that are internally consistent
Shows correct algebraic simplification ending in the constant 9
Verifies correctly using the starting number 15

concepts.name: Two-variable algebra: the date-guessing trick
concepts.description: Representing the date-guessing trick using two letter-numbers, month M and day D, and decoding a reported final answer back into the original date.
concepts.idea: When a trick depends on two separate pieces of information, here the month and the day, algebra needs two letters, and the final expression combines both; a friend's single reported number can still be decoded because of how the digits of M and D sit within it.
concepts.rule: For the date trick, multiply the month M by 5 to get 5M, add 6 to get 5M+6, multiply by 4 to get 20M+24, add 9 to get 20M+33, multiply by 5 to get 100M+165, then add the day D to get 100M+165+D. To decode a reported total, subtract 165: the last two digits of what remains give the day D, and whatever is left in front gives the month M.
concepts.example: For the date 26th January (M=1, D=26): 100(1)+165+26=291. Subtracting 165 from 291 gives 126; the last two digits, 26, give the day, and the remaining 1 gives the month, so it decodes back to 26th January.

questions.q: In the date-guessing trick, if M stands for the month number, what does 'multiply the month by 5' give?
questions.a: 5M

questions.q: Which of these is NOT equal to 5M + 6?
In the trick, after multiplying the month by 5, adding 6, and then multiplying by 4, the expression becomes ____.
The final expression in the date-guessing trick, after every step, is
Why does the date trick use two letters, M and D, instead of just one?
questions.a: Because the trick depends on two separate unknown quantities, the month and the day
o: Because the trick depends on two separate unknown quantities, the month and the day
Because the answer must always be a two-digit number
Because algebra rules require exactly two letters
Because M and D must always be equal

questions.q: In the final total 100M + 165 + D, why does the day D not get multiplied by any of the numbers in the trick?
questions.a: Because the day is only added at the very last step, after all the multiplications are already done
o: Because the day is only added at the very last step, after all the multiplications are already done
Because the day is always smaller than the month
Because days cannot be multiplied in algebra
Because only odd-numbered steps involve multiplication

questions.q: Explain why knowing that a day D is at most 31 (so at most two digits) lets us recover D from the final total after subtracting 165.
questions.a: Because D never needs more than two digits, whatever forms the last two digits of the number left after subtracting 165 must be D, and whatever comes before that must be the month M.
s: States that D is at most two digits since days go up to 31
Explains that the last two digits of (total - 165) are read off as D, leaving M in front

questions.q: A friend reports a final total of 482 for the date trick. What is 482 - 165?
Using 317 (the result of subtracting 165 from 482), decode the month and day the friend started with.
questions.a: The last two digits, 17, give the day D=17. The digit before that, 3, gives the month M=3, so the date is 17th March.
s: Reads off the last two digits as D = 17
Reads off the remaining digit as M = 3 and names the date, 17th March

questions.q: If the month is June (M=6) and the day is 9, what is 100M + 165 + D?
If the month is October (M=10) and the day is 4, the final total 100M+165+D equals ____.
If the month is December (M=12) and the day is 3, what is 100M + 165 + D?
A friend's final total for the date trick is 580. Decode the date.
questions.a: 580 - 165 = 415. The last two digits, 15, give the day, and the remaining digit, 4, gives the month, so the date is 15th April.
s: Subtracts 165 from 580 to get 415
Correctly reads off day = 15 and month = 4 (15th April)

questions.q: A friend's final total for the date trick is 1069. Decode the date.
questions.a: 1069 - 165 = 904. The last two digits, 04, give the day 4, and the remaining digit, 9, gives the month, so the date is 4th September.
s: Subtracts 165 from 1069 to get 904
Correctly reads off day = 4 and month = 9 (4th September)

questions.q: A friend changes the trick slightly: multiply the month by 5, add 6, multiply by 4, add 9, multiply by 5, add TWICE the day (instead of just the day). Find the new algebraic expression for the final total in terms of M and D, and explain what you would still need to subtract before reading off the date, and why the simple 'last two digits' read-off might now fail.
questions.a: Following the same steps as before but adding 2D at the end gives 100M + 165 + 2D. You would still subtract 165 first, but the remainder, 100M + 2D, no longer has D sitting cleanly in the last two digits since it is doubled; if D is large enough, the doubled value can carry into the digits used for the month, so the simple last-two-digits read-off can fail.
s: Re-derives the algebra correctly to reach 100M + 165 + 2D
States that 165 must still be subtracted first
Explains why doubling D can break the clean last-two-digit read-off, with a reason

questions.q: Assertion (A): From the final total of the date trick, subtracting 165 and then reading the last two digits always gives the day. Reason (R): since the day is at most 31, it never needs more than two digits, so it always occupies exactly the last two digits of (total - 165).
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Consider: (I) In the expression 100M + 165 + D, the coefficient of M is 100 because the month was multiplied by 5, then by 4, then by 5 again (5 x 4 x 5 = 100). (II) The day D also gets multiplied by 100 in the final expression, just like the month. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A student claims that because 100M + 165 + D is always at least 266 (using the smallest month M=1 and the smallest day D=1: 100+165+1=266), the trick cannot correctly be used to identify a month greater than 9. Test this claim using December (M=12, D=1) and explain whether it is correct.
questions.a: For December with D=1: 100(12)+165+1=1366. Decoding: 1366-165=1201; the last two digits, 01, give the day, and the remaining digits, 12, give the month, so it decodes correctly to 1st December. So the student's claim is wrong: the trick works for two-digit months just as well, because the coefficient 100 is exactly chosen to keep the day and month digits from overlapping regardless of the month's size.
s: Computes the total correctly for December with D=1 (1366)
Decodes it correctly back to M=12, D=01
Concludes the student's claim is false, with the reason that the coefficient 100 keeps month and day digits separate

questions.q: A student decodes a final total of 580 by subtracting 165 to get 415, then reads it as 'the 41st day of the 5th month'. Identify the mistake and give the correct date.
questions.a: The student split the digits from the wrong end: the LAST two digits (15) are the day, and what remains (4) is the month, not the first two digits. The correct date is 15th April.
s: Identifies that the digit split was taken from the wrong end (first two digits instead of last two)
Gives the correct date, 15th April

questions.q: Design your own version of the date trick using different numbers (not 5, 6, 4, 9, 5) so that the final expression still separates cleanly into 100M + (some constant) + D. Show your steps, the resulting algebraic expression, and encode and decode a date of your choosing.
questions.a: Example trick: multiply the month by 10, multiply by 10 again, add 50, then add the day. This gives 100M + 50 + D. For 8th July (M=7, D=8): 100(7)+50+8=758. To decode, subtract 50 to get 708; the last two digits, 08, give the day, and the remaining digit, 7, gives the month, so it decodes back to 8th July.
s: Designs valid steps whose multiplications combine to give coefficient 100 for M
States the correct resulting expression, 100M + 50 + D (or equivalent)
Demonstrates encoding and decoding correctly with a chosen date

concepts.name: Number pyramids: expressions for the top entry
concepts.description: Using the rule that each entry is the sum of the two entries directly below it to write algebraic expressions for the topmost entry of a pyramid, given letter-numbers in the bottom row.
concepts.idea: If the bottom row of a pyramid is written using letters, each row above can be built by adding neighbouring pairs, so the top entry becomes a single algebraic expression combining all the bottom letters.
concepts.rule: For a 2-row pyramid with bottom a, b, the top is a+b. For a 3-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c, the middle row is a+b and b+c, and the top is (a+b)+(b+c) = a+2b+c. For a 4-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c, d, the same rule repeats one row further to give a+3b+3c+d.
concepts.example: Bottom row 4, 1, 10: the middle row is 4+1=5 and 1+10=11; the top is 5+11=16, which matches a+2b+c = 4+2(1)+10 = 16.

questions.q: In a number pyramid, each entry equals
questions.a: the sum of the two numbers directly below it
o: the sum of the two numbers directly below it
the product of the two numbers directly below it
the difference of the two numbers directly below it
double the number directly below it

questions.q: For a 2-row pyramid with bottom entries a and b, the top entry is
questions.a: a + b

questions.q: For a 3-row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c, the middle row entries are a+b and ____.
questions.a: b + c

questions.q: Which of these is NOT equal to a + 2b + c, the top entry of a 3-row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c?
questions.a: a + b + c

questions.q: Why does the letter b appear twice (as 2b) in the simplified top entry of a 3-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c?
questions.a: Because b is used in both middle-row sums, a+b and b+c, so it gets added in twice when those are combined
o: Because b is used in both middle-row sums, a+b and b+c, so it gets added in twice when those are combined
Because b is always the largest number
Because the pyramid rule doubles the middle entry
Because a and c must always be equal to b

questions.q: In a 3-row pyramid, the middle row is a+b and b+c. What is their sum?
questions.a: a + 2b + c

questions.q: Explain, using the bottom row 4, 1, 10, why the top of the 3-row pyramid is 16, both by adding row by row and by using the expression a+2b+c.
questions.a: Row by row: the middle row is 4+1=5 and 1+10=11, so the top is 5+11=16. Using the expression with a=4, b=1, c=10: a+2b+c = 4+2+10=16, which matches.
s: Correctly builds the pyramid row by row to get 16
Correctly substitutes into a+2b+c and confirms it also gives 16

questions.q: For a 4-row pyramid with bottom row a, b, c, d, which expression correctly gives the topmost entry?
questions.a: a + 3b + 3c + d

questions.q: Show that for the 4-row pyramid with bottom row 1, 3, 3, 1, the top entry given by a+3b+3c+d equals 20, and verify this by building the pyramid row by row.
questions.a: Row by row: bottom 1, 3, 3, 1 gives the next row 4, 6, 4; then 10, 10; then the top, 20. Using a+3b+3c+d = 1+3(3)+3(3)+1 = 1+9+9+1 = 20, which matches.
s: Builds the pyramid correctly row by row to reach the top value 20
Substitutes correctly into a+3b+3c+d and confirms it also equals 20

questions.q: Using a+2b+c for a 3-row pyramid, what is the top entry when the bottom row is 5, 2, 6?
The bottom row of a 2-row pyramid is 9 and 14. The top entry is ____.

Computes 12 + 2(7) + 3 = 29 correctly

questions.q: Without building the entire pyramid, find the top of a 4-row pyramid whose bottom row is 6, 4, 9, 2, using the expression a+3b+3c+d. Show your substitution and the final answer, then check your answer by building the first two rows above the bottom.
questions.a: a+3b+3c+d = 6+3(4)+3(9)+2 = 6+12+27+2 = 47. Checking: the row above the bottom is 6+4=10, 4+9=13, 9+2=11; the next row is 10+13=23, 13+11=24; the top is 23+24=47, which matches.
s: Substitutes correctly into a+3b+3c+d to get 47
Shows correct working of the substitution arithmetic
Verifies by building at least two rows of the pyramid and reaching the same top value

questions.q: Assertion (A): In a 3-row pyramid, the middle letter b of the bottom row contributes more to the top entry than a or c do. Reason (R): the simplified top entry is a + 2b + c, so b is multiplied by 2 while a and c are each multiplied by 1.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Consider: (I) In a 4-row pyramid with bottom a, b, c, d, the coefficient of a in the top entry is always 1, no matter how many rows the pyramid has. (II) In a 4-row pyramid, b and c always have the same coefficient as each other in the top entry. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: A student says that doubling every number in the bottom row of a 3-row pyramid will always exactly double the top entry. Test this using the bottom rows 2, 1, 5 and then 4, 2, 10 (double of the first), and explain algebraically why this is true in general.
questions.a: For 2, 1, 5: a+2b+c = 2+2+5=9. For 4, 2, 10: a+2b+c = 4+4+10=18, exactly double 9. Algebraically, if every bottom entry doubles (a, b, c become 2a, 2b, 2c), the top entry becomes 2a+2(2b)+2c = 2(a+2b+c), which is exactly double the original top entry, so the student is correct.
s: Computes the top entry for both bottom rows correctly (9 and 18)
Notes that 18 is exactly double 9
Gives the correct algebraic reason: 2a+4b+2c = 2(a+2b+c)

questions.q: A student says the top of a 3-row pyramid with bottom row 3, 6, 2 is a+b+c = 3+6+2 = 11. Identify the mistake and give the correct top entry.
questions.a: The student used a+b+c instead of the correct formula a+2b+c, forgetting that the middle letter b is counted twice. The correct top entry is 3+2(6)+2=17.
s: Identifies that the student used the wrong formula (b not doubled)
Gives the correct top entry, 17

questions.q: Design a 3-row number pyramid (choose your own three bottom numbers) whose top entry is exactly 50. Show the bottom row you chose, the algebraic substitution into a+2b+c, and verify by building the pyramid row by row.
questions.a: Example: choose bottom row 10, 15, 10. a+2b+c = 10+30+10=50. Row by row: the middle row is 10+15=25 and 15+10=25; the top is 25+25=50, which matches.
s: Chooses a valid bottom row and correctly substitutes into a+2b+c
Shows the substitution correctly equals 50
Verifies by building the pyramid row by row and reaching 50

concepts.name: Solving pyramids and grids by setting up equations
concepts.description: Using the pyramid or grid rule together with given totals to form and solve linear equations for unknown entries, including the Calendar Magic 2x2 grid and shape-based Algebra Grids.
concepts.idea: When some entries of a pyramid or grid are unknown but their relationships and one or more totals are known, the pyramid or grid rule turns into equations that can be solved for the unknowns, exactly as with any letter-number puzzle.
concepts.rule: Write each known relationship as an equation (for a pyramid: upper equals the sum of the two below; for Calendar Magic: a 2x2 grid's entries are a, a+1, a+7, a+8, so their sum is 4a+16; for Algebra Grids: each row's shapes sum to the value given in the last column), then solve the resulting equation or equations for the unknown letter or shape.
concepts.example: In a pyramid with top 60 and bottom-left 12, so a+b=60, 12+c=a, c+8=b, substituting gives (12+c)+(c+8)=60, so 20+2c=60, c=20.

questions.q: In the Calendar Magic 2x2 grid, if the top-left number is a, what are the other three numbers in the grid (using a normal calendar with 7 days in a row)?
In an Algebra Grid, what does the last column of each row represent?
questions.a: The sum of the shape-values in that row
o: The sum of the shape-values in that row
The product of the shape-values in that row
The largest shape-value in that row
The number of shapes in that row

questions.q: If three squares in a row sum to 27, then one square is worth ____.

concepts.name: Arranging digits for the largest product
concepts.description: Placing three distinct one-digit numbers into a 2-digit x 1-digit multiplication to obtain the largest possible product, and the algebraic reasoning that proves which arrangement wins.
concepts.idea: With three digits to place into two boxes forming a 2-digit number, and one box forming the multiplier, only six arrangements are possible; comparing them systematically, and by expanding algebraically, shows the largest digit should be the 1-digit multiplier, and the remaining two digits should be arranged in decreasing order in the 2-digit multiplicand.
concepts.rule: For three distinct digits p<q<r, the largest product among all six arrangements of the form (2-digit) x (1-digit) is qp x r: put the largest digit r alone as the multiplier, and arrange the other two digits in decreasing order (q then p) as the multiplicand.
concepts.example: For digits 2, 3, 5: the six products are 23x5, 25x3, 32x5, 35x2, 52x3, 53x2. The largest is 32x5=160, matching the rule (largest digit 5 as multiplier, remaining digits 3, 2 in decreasing order).

o: Placing the largest digit in the tens place of the multiplicand

concepts.name: Decoding divisibility tricks using algebra
concepts.description: Writing 2-digit and 3-digit numbers algebraically to prove why certain digit-reversal, digit-sum and digit-repeating tricks always produce a multiple of 9, 11, 37 or 1001.
concepts.idea: A 2-digit number ab really means 10a+b, and its reverse ba means 10b+a; subtracting or adding these expressions and factoring reveals a hidden common factor, which is why the trick's result is always divisible by that factor, whatever digits were chosen.
concepts.rule: For a 2-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b (b>a), reversing and subtracting gives (10b+a)-(10a+b) = 9(b-a), always a multiple of 9. Adding instead gives (10a+b)+(10b+a) = 11(a+b), always a multiple of 11. For a 3-digit number abc = 100a+10b+c, cycling its digits to bca and cab and adding all three gives 111(a+b+c) = 3x37x(a+b+c), always a multiple of 37 (and of 3). Repeating a 3-digit number abc to form the 6-digit number abcabc is the same as abc x 1001, and since 1001 = 7x11x13, dividing successively by 7, 11 and 13 always returns abc.
concepts.example: For the 2-digit number 47: reversed is 74; the difference 74-47=27=9x3, matching 9(7-4)=27.

questions.a: 123+231+312=666. 666/9=74 exactly, so it is indeed divisible by 9 here. Algebraically, the sum of a number and its two rotations is always 111(a+b+c) = 3x37x(a+b+c).
